tier_reason: The paper is peer-reviewed (IEEE TDSC 2025, DOI 10.1109/TDSC.2025.3575915; arXiv 2306.01989v3). It states gcc-9.4.0, the flags and an i7-11700F, and compares against the pq-crystals AVX2 code (Tables IX and XI). It falls short of A because the repo's per-variant test/test_speed.c harness only covers the authors' own Round 3 AVX2/AVX-512 code (Dilithium2 sk = 2528 bytes). The repo ships neither a clearly identified unmodified pq-crystals/NIST AVX2 baseline nor the FIPS 204 ML-DSA code behind the headline Table XI numbers.

corrections.baseline: pq-crystals/dilithium AVX2 implementation: the 'standard' branch (FIPS 204 ML-DSA) AVX2 code for the headline Table XI numbers, and the NIST Round 3 submission AVX2 code for Table IX. This is the upstream code that liboqs/PQClean also derive from; liboqs and PQClean were not benchmarked directly.
corrections.claimed_speedup: Cycle-count reductions of AVX-512 vs the pq-crystals FIPS 204 AVX2 code (Table XI) for ML-DSA-44/65/87: KeyGen 43.2%/39.3%/45.6%, Sign 36.6%/41.6%/43.7%, Verify 45.3%/46.5%/47.4%. For example, ML-DSA-44 KeyGen drops from 84270 to 47760 cycles. That is about 1.58x-1.90x faster (derived from page data). Against the NIST Round 3 AVX2 code (Table IX), Dilithium2/3/5 cycle reductions are 50.0%-65.1%, about 2.0x-2.9x (derived from page data). Within both the AVX2 and the AVX-512 implementations, PSPM cuts c·s / c·e multiplication cycles by 47%-66% versus NTT (Table VI, Dilithium3).
corrections.workload: Round 3 Dilithium2/3/5 and FIPS 204 ML-DSA-44/65/87 KeyGen, Sign and Verify cycle counts on one core (median of 100000 runs). PSPM(-TEE) replaces NTT for the small-polynomial products (c·s, c·e) in both the AVX2 and AVX-512 implementations, not only on the AVX-512 path. Metric is per-operation cycles (latency).
corrections.compiler_and_flags: gcc-9.4.0 with -Wshadow -Wpointer-arith -mavx2 -mavx512f -mavx512vbmi -mavx512bw -mavx512cd -mavx512vl -mpopcnt -maes -march=native -mtune=native -O3. The paper prints the AVX-512 flags as '-mAVX-512F' etc.; the repo Makefiles use -mavx512*.
corrections.hardware: Intel Core i7-11700F (Rocket Lake) at 2.5 GHz, TurboBoost and Hyper-Threading disabled, Ubuntu 20.04
corrections.caveats: The repo has no LICENSE file (GitHub license null), so it is reference-only. The code derives from the NIST reference Dilithium and PQClean, but the repo itself grants no license. The repo describes itself as 'the source code of the paper Optimizing Dilithium Implementation with AVX2/-512', but the arXiv v3 PDF still says 'We will later open source our code' and does not link it. The owner xurq5953 does not match a listed author name, so the attribution rests on the repo's own statement. The repo holds Round 3 Dilithium only (Dilithium2 sk 2528 bytes), so the headline ML-DSA numbers in the abstract/Table XI cannot be reproduced from it. The percentages are cycle reductions, not throughput increases. The paper says the implementation is not fully constant-time-audited. It also notes that some hash functions are not yet vectorized.

notes: Downgraded A->B: the paper is peer-reviewed and its methodology is complete, but the artifact repo lacks the baseline and the ML-DSA variant the claimed numbers come from. All claimed percentages appear verbatim in the abstract and Table XI. Metadata checked: 3 stars, not a fork, not archived, last commit 2025-07-16 (stale), no license, so usability is corrected from 'mixed' to 'reference'.

tier_reason: The peer-reviewed paper (CHES 2011, and J. Cryptographic Engineering 2012, DOI 10.1007/s13389-012-0027-1) reports eBATS cycle counts on hydra2 (Xeon E5620, Turbo Boost off). It compares them with eBATS ecdonaldp256 (ECDSA P-256) on the same machine. The paper states no compiler or flags, and the 2011 hydra2 eBATS pages were not opened, so the tier is B, not A.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Signing: 87548 cycles vs ecdonaldp256 (OpenSSL-based ECDSA P-256) at 1790936 cycles, ~20.5x faster (derived from page data). Single-signature verification: 273364 vs 2087500 cycles, ~7.6x faster (derived from page data). Batch verification of 64 signatures takes 8.55 million cycles (under 134000 cycles/signature), ~15.6x faster than ecdonaldp256 verification (derived from page data). All figures are on hydra2 (Xeon E5620, Westmere).
corrections.hardware: Intel Xeon E5620 (Westmere, 2.4 GHz), eBATS machine 'hydra2', Turbo Boost disabled
corrections.caveats: The paper does not say ecdonaldp256 uses OpenSSL; it only says 'ECDSA signatures using the NIST P-256 elliptic curve'. The OpenSSL basis is confirmed by current eBATS, which lists ecdonaldp256 implementations 'openssl' and 'opensslnew' (code calls EC_KEY_new). The paper does not state compiler or flags. The hydra2 figures come from the radix-2^51 / 30KB-table code that the paper targets at Westmere (i.e. amd64-51-30k, inferred from Sections 3-4), not the radix-2^64 amd64-64-24k variant, which the paper says bottlenecks on Nehalem/Westmere. The numbers are 2011-era; the implementations still ship in SUPERCOP and are still benchmarked on eBATS alongside the newer lib25519 code. The software is a public-domain dedication with no patent grant; the authors say they have not been notified of any patent claims.

notes: All numbers check out in the paper intro; the only fixes are marking the ratios as derived and correcting the claim that the paper calls ecdonaldp256 OpenSSL. The record name's 'amd64-64-24k' label is likely wrong for the Westmere figures, which point to amd64-51-30k. maintenance_status changed from 'finished' to 'abandoned' because the authors give no completion statement and the software page was last revised 2017-01-22; the code is still distributed in SUPERCOP 20260831.

tier_reason: The peer-reviewed ASIACRYPT 2015 paper (extended ePrint 2015/565) Table 5 compares FourQlib 2.0 against the Gueron-Krasnov P-256 code [27] and Curve25519, with CPU models and TurboBoost-off stated. It falls short of A because no compiler or flags are given. Also, the P-256 figures were copied from [27] rather than measured by the FourQ authors on their own machines.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Table 5 (ePrint 2015/565): variable-base scalar multiplication up to 5.6x faster than the Gueron-Krasnov P-256 implementation [27] (Sandy Bridge 72k vs 400k cycles; Haswell 56k vs 312k). One ephemeral DH round is up to 4.4x faster than P-256 (Sandy Bridge 112k vs 490k). Variable-base is 2.2-2.9x faster than the Curve25519 implementations [3,14], and ephemeral DH 1.9-3.7x faster.
corrections.caveats: The P-256 comparison figures (Sandy Bridge and Haswell only) were copied directly from the Gueron-Krasnov paper [27], not re-measured on the FourQ authors' machines. That code is the basis of OpenSSL's ecp_nistz256, whose header credits Gueron and Krasnov. The paper states no compiler or flags, only CPU models. The benchmark CPUs are 2011-2015-era. No SchnorrQ signing/verification cycle comparison against a baseline appears in the paper, which covers scalar multiplication and DH only. The core is MIT-licensed, but the ARM folders include CC0 wrappers and LGPL-3.0 libopencm3.

notes: All claimed ratios match the paper text and Table 5. The DH-vs-Curve25519 range (1.9-3.7x) was added, and the claim that the numbers 'predate OpenSSL's nistz256 merge' was dropped as unverified. Metadata checked: MIT, 95 stars, not a fork, not archived, last commit 2022-08-31 (abandoned).
